common_name: Kidd's Climax Dahlia (Giant Blush Pink-Lavender-Cream Formal Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; Kidd's Climax has remained a top exhibition favorite for decades thanks to its enormous formal decorative blooms.

directions: Set tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep in rich, well-drained soil once the ground has warmed, and stake well before the plant reaches full size. Kidd's Climax carries colossal formal decorative flowers that blend soft pink, lavender, and creamy yellow tones in a single bloom, often confused for the similarly colored 'Strawberry Ice'. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and disbud side shoots if show-quality blooms are the goal, since the massive flower heads otherwise compete with each other for energy. Lift tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8 and store them in a cool, dry place over winter.
sources: Old House Gardens — heirloom bulb notes

common_name: Chat Noir Dahlia (Deep Red Spiky Semi-Cactus Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Chat Noir, French for 'black cat', produces narrow, twisting deep red petals typical of semi-cactus dahlias.

directions: Plant tubers with the eye facing upward and stake plants early, since Chat Noir's tall stems can reach shoulder height by midsummer. The semi-cactus blooms carry long, slightly twisted, deep velvety red petals that give the flower a spiky, dramatic silhouette rather than the flat, rounded look of decorative types. Deadhead regularly through the season to keep new buds forming, and watch for its long, sturdy stems, which make it a reliable choice for cutting. This French-bred variety has held up as a garden and show favorite for decades thanks to its rich color and consistent flower form.

common_name: Akita Dahlia (Crimson-Red Novelty Dahlia with White-Tipped Petals)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed; Akita is a novelty fully-double dahlia with chrysanthemum-like petals shading from dark crimson to yellow at the base, each tipped in white.

directions: Set tubers horizontally with the growth eye up, and pinch the central shoot when the plant reaches about a foot tall to build a bushier, more floriferous habit. Akita's fully double flowers resemble a chrysanthemum bloom more than a typical dahlia, with narrow crimson-red petals that blend to yellow near the base and carry distinct white tips, giving each flower a frosted, two-tone look. This long-admired novelty-type dahlia has a devoted exhibition following for the clarity and consistency of its unusual coloring. Stake plants as they gain height, since the fully double blooms are heavier than they first appear.

common_name: Zorro Dahlia (Giant Dark Red Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Zorro produces some of the largest blooms among giant decorative dahlias, so stake plants well before flowering begins.

directions: Give Zorro plenty of room and a sturdy stake driven in at planting time, since its very large, deep red decorative blooms can weigh down unsupported stems. For the biggest exhibition flowers, stop the central growing tip after four or five leaf pairs and limit side shoots to a few per plant, though leaving the plant undisbudded still produces a generous garden display. The intensely dark red color holds well through the heat of summer and makes a strong focal point in borders or cutting beds. Regular deadheading keeps the long bloom season going from midsummer until frost.

common_name: Edinburgh Dahlia (Purple and White Bicolor Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed; Edinburgh bears small, fully double flowers in rich purple that shade to white at the petal tips.

directions: Plant tubers with the eye facing up in a sunny, sheltered spot, and provide a stake early since the upright, bushy habit still benefits from support once flowers open. Edinburgh's compact, fully double flowers show a vivid purple that fades to crisp white at the petal edges, producing a striking bicolor effect against the plant's mid-green foliage. It blooms freely from midsummer into autumn and responds well to regular deadheading, which keeps new buds coming right up to first frost. The relatively small flower size makes it easy to work into mixed borders and cutting gardens alike.

common_name: Hillcrest Royal Dahlia (Deep Purple-Red Cactus Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Hillcrest Royal carries medium-sized cactus blooms with an abundance of narrow, incurved purplish-red florets.

directions: Set tubers horizontally with the eye up in fertile, humus-rich soil, and stake plants as they grow since the upright, clump-forming habit carries numerous flowering stems. Hillcrest Royal produces fully double cactus-type blooms packed with slender, incurving florets in a rich, deep purplish-red that holds its color well through the season. The strong stems and reliable flower form have made it a long-running favorite for both garden display and the show bench. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to maintain a steady flush of new flowers from early summer through the first hard frost.

common_name: Downham Royal Dahlia (Claret-Purple Miniature Ball Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed; Downham Royal forms neat, tightly rolled miniature ball blooms in a rich claret-purple that read as velvety in both sun and shade.

directions: Plant tubers with the growth eye facing up and stake plants early, since the long, strong stems are a major asset for cutting but still benefit from support in windy sites. Downham Royal's small, perfectly rounded blooms are built from tightly inrolled petals in a deep claret-purple that looks rich and velvety whether viewed in bright sun or dappled shade. Deadhead through the season to keep the compact flowers coming, and expect a long bloom window that runs from midsummer well into fall. Its small, uniform flower size and sturdy stems make it especially well suited to bouquets and mixed arrangements.

common_name: Mick's Peppermint Dahlia (White Semi-Cactus Dahlia Splashed with Hot Pink)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Mick's Peppermint produces huge white semi-cactus blooms splashed and flecked with hot pink, with no two flowers patterned exactly alike.

directions: Give Mick's Peppermint generous spacing and a sturdy stake, since its huge semi-cactus flowers are both heavy and eye-catching once fully open. Each bloom is predominantly white but splashed, streaked, or flecked with vivid hot pink in a pattern that varies from flower to flower, giving the plant a lively, ever-changing look through the season. Pinch young plants to encourage a bushier frame able to support the large flower heads, and deadhead regularly to keep fresh blooms coming. It performs equally well as a garden specimen or a conversation-starting cut flower.

common_name: Weston Spanish Dancer Dahlia (Yellow-and-Red Bicolor Cactus Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed; Weston Spanish Dancer carries cactus-form blooms that are pale yellow at the base and shade to deep red at the petal tips.

directions: Plant tubers with the eye up in fertile, well-drained soil, and water consistently through the season, since this cultivar prefers steadier moisture than many dahlia types. The narrow, pointed cactus-form petals open pale yellow near the base and flame outward into deep red at the tips, giving each flower a warm, sunset-like gradient that is distinctive on the show bench and in the border alike. Stake plants as they grow to support the medium-sized but numerous blooms produced over a long season. Regular deadheading keeps the display going strong from midsummer through the first frost.

common_name: Chimacum Troy Dahlia (Deep Burgundy Miniature Ball Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Chimacum Troy is a reliable miniature ball dahlia popular with cut-flower growers for its deep burgundy-wine color and uniform blooms.

directions: Pinch Chimacum Troy when it reaches about a foot tall to encourage strong branching, since this variety is grown as much for its long, straight stems as for its flowers. The tightly formed miniature ball blooms open a deep burgundy-maroon with hints of dark purple, reading almost like rich red wine or velvet in the garden. It is a dependable, heavy-flowering plant often described as a workhorse by cut-flower growers, producing uniform blooms on strong stems well suited to bouquets. Keep up with deadheading and harvesting to encourage continuous production through the season.

common_name: Wootton Cupid Dahlia (Soft Pink Ball Dahlia with Pale Yellow Centers)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed; Wootton Cupid produces clear, soft pink ball-form flowers with a faint lemon-yellow glow toward the center.

directions: Set tubers horizontally with the eye facing up in fertile, humus-rich soil, and stake plants as they reach their full height, since this is a taller ball-type variety. The fully double, spherical flowers are a soft, clear pink that lightens to a pale lemon-yellow glow near the center, giving the blooms a gentle, two-tone softness compared to the more saturated colors of many ball dahlias. It flowers reliably from midsummer into fall with regular deadheading, and the neat, rounded bloom form holds up well as a cut flower. Divide and store tubers over winter in colder zones to maintain vigor the following season.

common_name: Pink Giraffe Dahlia (Pink Orchid-Type Dahlia Speckled with White)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Pink Giraffe is a long-grown novelty orchid-type dahlia with pink petals speckled and splashed with white, reminiscent of a giraffe's coat pattern.

directions: Plant tubers with the eye facing up in ordinary, moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, and stake plants once they begin to bulk up, since even this moderate-height variety benefits from light support in exposed sites. The long, incurved and spreading petals open a warm pink dappled and spotted with white in a pattern that gave the cultivar its name, with no two flowers quite identical. It blooms over an unusually long season, from midsummer until frost, and the distinctive mottled coloring makes it a conversation piece wherever it is planted. Deadhead regularly to keep new buds forming and the display going strong into autumn.
